quiz_item.question: In Fish and Wildlife Management Requirement 1, what does 'carrying capacity' mean for a wildlife habitat, and how do regulated hunting and fishing seasons support conservation?
options: A. Carrying capacity is the maximum weight of fish a single angler can carry in a creel, and wildlife agencies ban all habitat restoration.

B. Carrying capacity is the maximum population of a given species that a habitat's food, water, cover, and space can sustainably support year-round without degrading the ecosystem; science-based harvest limits and excise taxes on sporting gear (Pittman-Robertson and Dingell-Johnson Acts) fund habitat conservation and prevent overpopulation starvation.
C. Carrying capacity measures the number of paved roads inside a national park, and wildlife management relies on introducing invasive species to replace native predators.
D. Carrying capacity never changes between summer and winter, so removing all predators permanently guarantees unlimited herd health.

(b) Conduct a creel census on a small lake to estimate catch per unit effort and report the results to your counselor. (c) Examine the stomach contents of three fish and record the findings. Include at least four species of native plants and four species of animal life, such as whirligig beetles, freshwater shrimp, tadpoles, water snails, and golden shiners. After 60 days of observation, discuss with your counselor the life cycles, food chains, and management needs you have recognized. Before completing this requirement, check local laws on releasing these organisms back into the wild, and follow your counselor's direction in disposing of these organisms humanely and safely.
